doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

chapter: Rock and roll, Elvis and Sinatra
title: Lieber and Stoller on Elvis and Memphis black music
summary: Story of Hound Dog's royalties during the Andrea Doria sinking, and Lieber and Stoller's surprise at Elvis's knowledge of black music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know, Lieber and Stoller talk about when I think one of them was on one of these ocean liners and it went down.

The Andrea Doria, right. And so the one of them, I can’t remember if it was Jerry or Mike, was on the ship. And so it went down as the ship was coming in. And I know they lost a lot of people. And he goes oh my God, I hope he’s okay. And as soon as he got there, oh thanks, blah, blah, blah. And then he tells them, once he tells him he’s alive, he goes, “Hey by the way,” you know, “we’ve got a big hit.” He goes, you know, because this was a couple of years later after she did it. He goes, “Yeah, it’s ‘Hound Dog.’” He goes, “Mama Thornton!” He goes, “No, no, this new guy, Elvis Presley.” He goes, “Elvis Presley’s got a hit?” He goes, “Yeah.” He goes, “We’ve got a number one hit. We’re going to get some nice royalties out of this.” And so, you know, they kind of put him down at the time because you know, it was just this kid with the hair and everything. Well when Elvis started doing the films he wanted Lieber and Stoller to write for him for all those films. That was great, because it was like eight, nine songs a film, and what Jerry said, and in the recent book that came out, he said, “we thought we were the hippest white kids in America.” You know, “we were dating black girls and everything. We had the jargon down” you know. “We wrote for the Robins and Charles Brown.” And he says, “This guy knew more about black music than we did.” Because he grew up in
Memphis and he would go see uh, what’s his name, the guy who did, the black piano player who married the one girl and slapped her around, oh God.

And Ike used to leave, it was in the black section of town, because he was always going down to the black section of town without telling mama. He goes, boy there was an alley in this place where Ike was playing in the afternoon matinees. And he would open the door and Elvis then could peer in and watch him play the piano. And he says, “Oh we knew Elvis was a hip little cat, man, at that time, he just loved our music, he loved our music.” And so he knew about white Gospel, black Gospel. He knew about the great singers like Billy Eckstine and the Ink Spots. He was hungry for music. You know? So he was a lot hipper than people give him credit — he just was not an articulate guy. But he had absorbed all this stuff. And when Jerry Lieber said that, he used to say, “Listen, we thought we were ten times hipper than him. When we worked with him he was just a teenager, you know, rock & roll pop star, but we had some real doubts.” Not intellect, you know, like a well-read person, but a sound person. So they were quite surprised after working with him.
